Sohrawardî and the Platonists of Persia
Chapter I A Life’s Great Undertaking
In Iran, Sohrawardî is traditionally known as shaykh al-Ishrâq: the shaykh, or learned master, of Ishrâq.
That last word, both the name and the emblem of his teaching, has become inseparable from the name of the master himself.
Literally, it means the rising of the sun, aurora consurgens, the light of morning.
The adjective ishrâqî describes what belongs to the dawn or the East, what shines with the splendor of morning, like the sun as it rises.
Ishrâqî-namâz is the morning prayer, corresponding to “Prime” among the traditional Christian hours of prayer.
The ishrâqî teaching is a theosophia matutina: a wisdom of the morning. The Ishrâqîyûn are all the thinkers and spiritual seekers who embrace this teaching.
We shall soon see how Sohrawardî unfolds the different meanings of this East and makes it the emblem of Iranian spirituality.
We shall also see how and why his teaching has a deep affinity with Shiite theosophy—an affinity at first concealed, then openly acknowledged.
Many Shiite thinkers have belonged to the Ishrâqîyûn.
Their case illustrates, more clearly than almost any other, the fate of philosophical reflection in Islam.
After Avicenna (d. 428 AH / 1037 CE), there came, on the one hand, Ghazâlî's critique of philosophy (d. 505 AH / 1111 CE).
More than one Western historian, struck by superficial similarities, has compared this critique with Kant's.

Ghazâlî’s critique was taken to mean that metaphysics was no longer possible—as though the withdrawal of one philosopher, or several, were enough to persuade everyone else to abandon the questions that have always made metaphysics indispensable to human beings. Unfortunately, this understanding of what has been called the “philosophical adventure” was confined rather too narrowly to the horizons of the West. The consequences of Ghazâlî’s critique were sought in the ultimately fruitless efforts of Averroes (d. 595/1198) in Andalusia.

After Averroes, what for so long was called “Arabic” philosophy—a regrettable error of perspective—seemed to disappear into the sands, while Latin Averroism flourished in the West. This view lost sight of what else had happened after Avicenna: during Averroes’ own lifetime, and in striking contrast to him, the immense work of Ibn ’Arabî was taking shape, a work that would nourish the spirituality of the Islamic East down to our own time; and in Iran, Avicenna’s philosophy was being transformed into the “Eastern philosophy” that was Sohrawardî’s achievement.

The great undertaking of Sohrawardî’s life, as he understood it and as his disciples have understood it from generation to generation, was less the ambition of a “founder” than that of a man bringing something back to life. His purpose was to revive the spiritual vision of ancient Persia, and it was in pursuing this purpose that he would say he had had no predecessor.

We must be clear about what this means. Zoroastrianism still existed in Iran, as it does today. There was no need to “revive” it, and Sohrawardî never presented himself as a Zoroastrian, a convert, or a reformer of Mazdean religion. Born into Islam, he remained a moslim and a mu’min—a Muslim and a believer—for it was within Islam itself that he found the place from which to undertake his work.

As he himself makes clear, his calling and his role were first of all those of a philosopher. In Isfahan he encountered a philosophical world in which Avicenna’s memory was still alive. He does not tell us precisely when he came to know Sufism, though his treatises bear witness to his personal experience of it. Nor does he tell us exactly what he knew of Shiite theosophy and its understanding of prophecy, traces of which can be found in his writings and which, in the end, help explain why he was brought to trial in Aleppo.

What he does confide, in his principal work, is that a sudden illumination revealed to him the meaning and sources of ancient Persian wisdom. From that vision sprang the undertaking that would henceforth claim all his energies. It enabled him to bring together the names of Plato and Zarathustra—Zoroaster—some three centuries before the great Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon (d. between 1450 and 1464) attempted a similar enterprise.

Yet Sohrawardî did not experience this undertaking as a struggle against Islam, even though it could not have been conceived within the limits of a strictly literal religion concerned only with outward observance. Quite the contrary: the energies of mystical faith, of the spiritual Islam alive within him, made it possible for him to embrace the undertaking and bring it to completion.

Inspired by the prophetic spirit of Islam, Sohrawardî came to see that ta’wîl—the interpretation that uncovers the hidden meaning of divine revelations—could also embrace the meaning of Zoroastrian prophecy, a meaning that only such an interpretation could disclose. We have seen how Shiite theosophy, through its idea of walâyat, the spiritual guardianship and authority entrusted to the friends of God, enters into the meaning of the missions of the prophets who came before the “Seal of the Prophets,” including the biblical prophets within its understanding of prophecy.

In a comparable way, Sohrawardî saw, in the radiance of the Light of Glory (the Xvarnah), glimpsed in turn at the “Lotus of the Utmost Boundary,” that the prophet and heroes of ancient Persia also belonged to the destinies traced out in the sacred history of the “Peoples of the Book.” In relation to the wisdom of ancient Zoroastrian Persia, he thus assumed something like the mediating role played by Salmân the Pure (Salmân Pâk, or Salmân the Persian, Salmân Pârsî) between the Iranian community and the Prophet’s Family (Ahl al-Bayt). As the Prophet himself is reported to have said, “Salmân is one of us, a member of our Household.”

The Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, would in their turn bring Sohrawardî’s themes into the family of Shiite theosophy. That is why his arrival in the philosophical and spiritual life of Islamic Persia mattered so profoundly, and left a mark that never disappeared. He too, while still young, was to seal the meaning of his cause with a martyr’s death, far from his native Iran, in Aleppo: the cause of the ’orafâ, the mystical seekers of divine wisdom, ever vulnerable to the hostility of the doctors of religious law when those doctors become rather too closely allied with the ambitions of political power.
We have already had occasion elsewhere to sketch the course of his life and work. An admiration dating from our youth led us to edit the collected texts of his treatises.
But books become scarce, or escape the attention of readers who are not specialists in Oriental studies. We must therefore outline the essentials once more here.

Shihâboddîn Yahyâ Sohrawardî, who must not be confused with the Sufis who bore the same name, was born, as his name indicates, at Sohraward around 549 AH (1155 CE). The town of Sohraward, south of Zenjân and west of Soltâniyeh, in the province of Jabal—the ancient Media—in northwestern Iran, was still a flourishing and populous place at that time, before the Mongol invasions. In the section on physics in one of his works, while discussing instances of petrification that he had himself observed, he expressly refers to his birthplace: “As we have observed,” he says, “in our own country ... near the town of Sohraward ...”
While still very young he went to study at Marâgheh, in Azerbaijan, under Shaykh Majdoddîn Gîlî.

Another of Gîlî’s pupils was Fakhroddîn Râzî, a celebrated name in the history of Islamic philosophy. Sohrawardî and Fakhroddîn Râzî later exchanged views, and some trace of their exchanges survives, but the contrast between these two thinkers could hardly have been greater. Fakhroddîn Râzî remained a distinguished representative of Islamic scholastic theology (Kalâm), placing his rational confidence in the methods of argument inherited from the Greek philosophers.

Sadrâ Shîrâzî, in his turn, as an Ishrâqî, would emphasize this contrast. According to Shahrazôrî, Sohrawardî’s faithful disciple and biographer, our shaykh seems to have had reservations about Fakhr Râzî’s philosophical abilities. Fakhr Râzî, by contrast, admired Sohrawardî without reserve. We are told that after Sohrawardî’s death a copy of his Talwîhât came into Fakhr Râzî’s hands, and that he reverently kissed the book.

After his studies at Marâgheh, Sohrawardî went to Isfahan, where, as we know, Avicenna had been active for several years. It was there that Sohrawardî encountered the Avicennian tradition. He studied closely a work by ’Omar ibn Sahlân Sâwajî, which he discusses repeatedly in one of his major books. Ibn Sahlân had written a commentary on Avicenna’s mystical treatise, the Epistle of the Bird, which Sohrawardî would himself translate into Persian. Also in Isfahan, he wrote one of his earliest Persian treatises for a group of friends.

Then began his wandering life, spent visiting Sufi communities and seeking the solitude in which meditation can ascend the stages of the mystical Path. He stayed at Diyâr Bakr, in southeastern Anatolia, where he was warmly received at the court of the Seljuks of Rûm. To one of them, ’Imâdoddîn Qarâ Arslân, emir of Kharpout, he dedicated a work entitled The Book of Tablets Dedicated to ’Imâdoddîn (Alwâh ’Imâdîyâ). What he was seeking in these long wanderings he reveals to us himself on the last page of one of his major books.

He was thus moving toward a destiny that one of his closest friends, Fakhroddîn Mardînî, had already foreseen. Speaking of Sohrawardî with their companions, Fakhr Mardînî had said: “What fire, what brilliance of dawn shines from this young man! Never in my life have I met anyone like him.

“Yet I fear the very excess of his ardour, his lack of caution in protecting himself. I fear that this may bring about his destruction.” An all too accurate premonition, alas. When news of Sohrawardî’s murder reached him, the same shaykh was able to say to his disciples: “Did I not predict it, when I was so anxious for him?”

It was after a long stay with his friend Fakhroddîn Mardînî at Diyâr Bakr that Sohrawardî travelled to Syria, to Aleppo, from which he would never return. Aleppo was then governed by al-Malik al-Zâhir, one of the sons of Salâhoddîn—the Saladin of Crusading history. Some of our chivalric romances have surrounded Saladin with a halo that, unfortunately, fades when we look at him from the Eastern side of the story. His fanaticism brought him into violent conflict with his own son over our shaykh al-Ishrâq. A deep and lasting friendship had quickly grown between the two young men, al-Malik al-Zâhir and Sohrawardî.

A few years later the great mystical theosopher Mohyiddîn Ibn ’Arabî would likewise become a close friend of this same son of Saladin. Meanwhile Shahrazôrî, Sohrawardî’s biographer, preserves an echo of the fierce disputes between Sohrawardî and the jurists, the doctors of the religious law known as foqahâ. Our young shaykh seems to have abandoned all caution, including the salutary practice of ketmân, the prudent concealment of esoteric beliefs. He appears to have spoken his mind openly, without concealing even the specialized terms in which he expressed his thought.

The charge brought against him by the doctors of the Law is particularly revealing if we recall what we said in the preceding book about Shiite teachings on prophecy and the Imams (above, Book I, Chapter VI). A brief, sharply worded exchange, preserved by a historian who seems in no way inclined to favour our shaykh, makes the accusation perfectly clear. “You have said in your books that God has the power to create a prophet whenever He wishes?”—“Certainly. God has power over all things.”—“But not the power to create a prophet.”—“Is that an absolute impossibility, or not?”—“You are a kâfir [an unbeliever].”

Thus the takfîr, the judgment declaring a person guilty of unbelief or infidelity to Islam, fell abruptly upon him. Of course, the force of a takfîr is limited, just as the authority claiming the right to pronounce it here is limited. It would be misleading to compare it with excommunication, which presupposes an institution such as the Church and the authority of a pope. Had Sohrawardî quietly moved somewhere else, the consequences would probably not have been tragic.
But such a flight was contrary to his deepest nature: his sense of loyalty, his readiness to challenge others, and his conviction that he served a cause greater than his personal interests.

The accusation admitted no distinctions. But how could one expect distinctions from the men making it? In fact, I know of no passage in which Sohrawardî states in so many words that God can create a prophet—a nabî—whenever He wishes, even after the coming of the one who was the “Seal of the Prophets.”

What we do find, however, is the prologue to his great book of Eastern Theosophy, which speaks of the hidden succession of a sacred line of sages possessed of divine wisdom (the silsilat al-’irfân), originating in the Qotb, the mystical pole around whom they are gathered. This prologue presupposes the original Shiite idea of the cycle of walâyat. Sohrawardî’s idea of a hidden spiritual lineage immediately calls to mind a text particularly characteristic of that idea: the conversation between the First Imam and his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyâd (above, Book I, Chapter III). Sohrawardî’s commentators recognized the connection: in explaining the prologue they quoted that conversation in full.

Nor did the ’olamâ, the scholars of religious law, fail to recognize what was at stake. They certainly did not see—and could not see—that the very succession of the cycle of walâyat presupposes the closure of lawgiving prophecy, and that there will be no more prophets sent to bring a new revealed law.

Nevertheless, something does continue afterwards, something that remains open to the future. It nourishes an entire spiritual life that refuses to treat religion simply as the observance of the Law, detached from its inward truth (haqîqat). This something is the “divine sap” that keeps the phenomenon of the sacred Book alive. Beneath the outer bark of the revealed text (zâhir), its hidden meaning (bâtin) continually rises and prepares new blossoms.

From this follow several ideas: that while the cycle of Revelation (wahy) given to lawgiving prophets is closed, the cycle of inspiration (ilhâm) remains open; that every outward form has an inward meaning and that ta’wîl, the interpretation of symbols, has a vital role to play; that concealed within the succession of walâyat is the continuation of a secret prophecy (nobowwat bâtinîya). This is no longer the mission of prophets sent to give laws, but is identical with the walâyat that, from the very beginning, from Adam onward, formed the inward dimension of every prophetic mission.

Finally, this inward meaning leads not, as has been superficially claimed, to the “relativity of all religions,” but to the integration of each religion in its own place within the hexaemeron, the “six days of Creation” of the religious cosmos as described by Nâsir-e Khosraw, one of the greatest Iranian Ismaili theosophers. The scholars of Aleppo may not have known all this explicitly, but they surely sensed enough of it to feel alarmed. In accusing Sohrawardî, they were by that very act identifying him as a representative of Shiism, or of a concealed Shiism, which at that time was more or less compelled to remain underground.

This was precisely the period when Saladin was fighting the Franks. Sunni power had also overcome the Fatimid dynasty of Cairo, which for more than two centuries had embodied the hopes of Ismaili esoteric Islam.

We have already recalled the paradox inherent in those hopes (above, Book I, Chapter II), and explained why the Twelver Shiite conception corresponded more closely to the metaphysical and spiritual essence of the Imamate, since it entailed the Twelfth Imam’s withdrawal into occultation (ghaybat) until the Last Day. It is equally certain that the sacred succession of the sages, and that of their Imam or mystical pole, are not worldly dynasties exercising political power in rivalry with other powers. Their relation to such powers resembles that of the dynasty of the guardians of the Grail to the official succession of the Apostolic See.

Yet perhaps a succession that is wholly hidden and spiritual seems, to the powerful of this world, not harmless but all the more threatening and alarming. For they can imagine no horizon beyond the one upon which the petty ambitions of earthly rule contend with one another.

It was therefore inevitable that a man like Saladin would listen closely to the reports of his ’olamâ. “If he is allowed to live,” they wrote of our young shaykh, “he will corrupt al-Malik al-Zâhir’s faith. If he is released, he will corrupt the whole country.” Saladin accordingly sent his son an order to put Sohrawardî to death.

But al-Malik al-Zâhir struggled desperately against it. Refusing to comply, he tried to shield his friend from the fury of the fanatics. The scholars again pressed Saladin, who sent a second letter to his son, threatening to strip him of the governorship of Aleppo if he refused. Three times the relentless accusers had to renew their demands before they could tear the shaykh away from al-Malik al-Zâhir’s protection. His biographers have never established exactly what happened at the end.

We do not know precisely how the young shaykh died. It is even possible that he voluntarily refused all food “until his Lord should see fit to call him back to Himself.” The date most commonly accepted for his death in the citadel of Aleppo is 5 Rajab 587 / 29 July 1191. He would have been thirty-six years old, or thirty-eight by the lunar calendar.

To historians who felt no particular attachment to him, he was the shaykh maqtûl—the slain, killed, or executed shaykh. To his disciples he was the shaykh shahîd, the martyr, the “true witness on the path of God.” To philosophers, the Ishrâqîyûn and others alike, he remains, by tradition, the shaykh al-Ishrâq.

Brief though his life was, and despite the disruptions of constant travel, Sohrawardî worked with extraordinary energy and produced a substantial body of writing. His biographer Shahrazôrî compiled the most complete list: about fifty works and shorter treatises in Arabic and Persian, most of which have come down to us. We cannot reproduce the full list here.
Let us simply recall that elsewhere we have divided the writings into four groups, according to their structure and purpose.

First comes a trilogy of three large, systematic treatises. As Sohrawardî conceived them, their purpose is above all preparatory: they equip the reader to study and put into practice a fourth work, the one containing the shaykh’s central teaching, the Book of Eastern Theosophy (Kitâb Hikmat al-Ishrâq). All three share the same structure, treating logic, physics, and metaphysics. They examine in detail the fundamental doctrines of Peripatetic philosophy—the Aristotelian tradition—as it was then taught within Islam. Sohrawardî always believed that familiarity with this philosophy was the necessary foundation and starting point of a philosopher’s education, even though the spiritual seeker was obliged to go beyond it. The three works generally maintain the severe tone of technical argument. Yet more than once the writing bursts open under the pressure of a lyrical inspiration, denouncing the wretchedness of those who are spiritually blind or anticipating the secret entrusted to the Book of Eastern Theosophy. We shall have much more to say about that book.

Next is a group of Opera minora, some eight shorter works in Arabic and Persian. Like the writings of the trilogy, each generally begins with an account of theoretical problems and ends at the threshold of mystical experience.

A third group forms a cycle of about ten short Persian works, cast as parables or stories of initiation. Together with the shaykh’s great book, these are the writings most characteristic of Sohrawardî’s spirituality. They are no longer teaching manuals but genuinely ’irfânî works, writings concerned with inward spiritual knowledge. The theoretical discussion has ended. Their purpose is to draw the reader into the movement of their “story,” to make it the reader’s own story, and so to lead the reader onto the Path. That is why we shall give them particular attention, translating two of them below.

Finally, standing apart, there is a collection of writings that together form a kind of “Book of Hours”: freely composed hymns that give liturgical expression to the Ishrâq. They include invocations addressed to archangelic powers, as well as exhortations and psalms inspired by visions of the last things. At times one can hear an echo of Manichaean devotion, as in this invocation: “Raise up the litany of Light, give victory to the people of Light, guide Light toward Light.”
2. The Lineage of the Ishrâqîyûn, or “Eastern” Theosophers

To understand fully what Sohrawardî intended and accomplished, one must read his great book, the Kitâb Hikmat al-Ishrâq. We have already devoted many years of work to this book, and we intend to publish a complete translation of it.

Yet such a translation cannot be separated from the work of the commentators who developed the ishrâqî doctrine in Iran, century after century. Inevitably, then, the translation as a whole will have to be extensive. Here we can only touch on the matter and recall why elsewhere we have translated the title as Theosophy of the Orient of Lights, or, more simply, The Book of Eastern Theosophy.

A few statements by the author are enough to convey the atmosphere of the book and suggest what our shaykh meant by the great family of Ishrâqîyûn, the “Eastern” theosophers, for whom he wrote the work that held the great undertaking of his young life. He closes it with these words: “Brothers, I entrust this book to your care.

“Watch over it; protect it from the unworthy, the profane. May it, by God, stand in my place among you as my successor [my ‘caliph’]. I finished composing it at the end of the month of Jomâdâ II in the year 582 of the Hegira, on the day when the seven planets were in conjunction in the sign of Libra.”

One of its commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî (d. 710/1310–1311 or 716/1316–1317), observes here that the date was Tuesday the twenty-ninth of that month—16 September 1186 in our calendar—and that the appearance of this magnificent book on that very day was among the effects of the extraordinary conjunction. Sohrawardî continues: “The Holy Spirit inspired this book in my heart all at once, on a marvellous day, although because of the difficulties caused by my travels I was unable to put it into writing until after several months.”

This was not, then, a book composed in the comfortable quiet of a scholar’s study. It came from a long period of gestation: reading, meditation, conversations while travelling slowly along the long roads of Iran and Anatolia, where chance made possible so many encounters and discoveries. And then, suddenly, came the “marvellous day” when the entire book, still in the form of an idea, rose before Sohrawardî’s mind. In that book his whole undertaking to establish a new theosophical vision at last took definite form, “under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit”—that is, of the angel Gabriel, who for the philosophers of Islam is both the Angel of Revelation and the Angel of Knowledge.

Certain pages of the great Trilogy already refer to this book, suggesting that he must have been writing the works side by side. Several allusions help us understand what he sought so feverishly, and why he undertook the long journeys recalled in the account of his life, despite the obstacles they placed in the way of writing. In the third work of the Trilogy, at the end of a long discussion of the problem of being, directed chiefly against the school of the Avicennian Ibn Sahlân, already mentioned here, Sohrawardî says: “These people have no means of escaping the difficulty, for the arguments we have set out at length admit of no trickery.

“The experienced investigator will become certain that the constructions advanced by these philosophers are utterly futile, and that all they are doing is wasting time. It is through the emergence of such philosophical speculations that wisdom—theosophy (hikmat)—is interrupted, the higher sciences of the spiritual Journey are erased, and the road to the Malakût, the spiritual kingdom, is closed. In the end, all that remains is heaps of writings.

“Yet there are people who, putting on the appearance of philosophers, allow themselves to be seduced by these things. They think that merely reading books can give a man a place among those who possess wisdom, without his having to enter the path of the spiritual world himself, without personally experiencing the vision of the spiritual Beings of Light.

“As for us, we have set down in a book what God revealed especially to us concerning these sublime sciences—things of which our predecessors were indeed given an overall glimpse, but which we have been granted the ability to unfold in detail. Their exposition will be found in our book entitled Eastern Theosophy. We have even invented a special script for this book, so that no one may become acquainted with its contents except the person approved by the Maintainer of the Book (Qayyim al-Kitâb), after the latter has verified that the necessary conditions are fulfilled.

“‘To whom God gives no light, what light shall he have?’ (Qur’an 24:40). For just as a mystic who lacks philosophical ability is incomplete, so too a philosopher who does not possess, along with his philosophy, a personal vision of the Signs and of the malakût is incomplete—a person not to be greatly esteemed, a man to whom the spiritual world has never spoken.”
Already this passage sets out the guiding thought of Sohrawardî’s fundamental work and the basic teaching of ishrâqî spirituality.

Another passage, from the conclusion of that same work, confirms it: “If the road toward God had not been cut off in our time, we would not have endured so much sadness, nor suffered the irritation of such grief. I am now approaching my thirtieth year. I have spent most of my life travelling, investigating, searching for a companion fully initiated into these things; but I have found no one informed about the Higher Sciences, nor anyone who believes in them.

“Brothers! This is the testament I leave you: let every concern other than the divine world fall away from you; let your only concern be perseverance in the work of mystical detachment (tajrîd). The key to all these things is placed in my book of Eastern Theosophy. Nowhere here have we dealt with them as we have dealt with them there.

“We even devised a special script for that book, to prevent its contents from becoming widely known. We believe that, even if the beginner cannot recognize its importance, the experienced investigator will at least understand that I have had no predecessor in writing such a book, and that it contains hidden dwelling places.”

We have found a trace of this secret script, to which the author has just referred twice, in at least one manuscript. It bears a strange resemblance to a secret alphabet used by the Ismailis. Is that merely a coincidence? The shaykh speaks of his solitary years, spent searching for a companion who shared his initiation. The search, he says, was in vain, so thoroughly had the field of the Higher Sciences been laid waste.

Yet had not the “Great Resurrection,” inaugurating a purely spiritual Islam, been proclaimed at the fortress of Alamût on 8 August 1164, in the mountains southwest of the Caspian Sea that Sohrawardî must have known? Might there not have been a possible companion there? We have also noted in passing the expression “Maintainer of the Book.” Sohrawardî may well have been looking far into the future, imagining something like an “Order of the Ishrâqîyûn” that would survive him, headed by an “Imam” who would hold his teaching in trust and initiate others into the secret of his Book of Eastern Theosophy.

But here we encounter another strange correspondence. The expression “Maintainer of the Book” is precisely the one used in Shiite hadith going back to the holy Imams, where it names the Imam’s essential function as guardian of the sacred Book’s secret interpretation: “the Book is the silent Imam, and the Imam is the speaking Book.” So a Shiite reader encountering this expression in Sohrawardî’s text could quite naturally understand it as referring to the Imam. And a Shiite of Sohrawardî’s own day would have shared his grief at the devastation of the Higher Sciences.

We cannot fail to take these signs seriously; others will come to support them. Both passages seem to point toward a final secret, whose key must be sought from the person who maintains and guards the Book—as though the boldness of what the book already states concealed an undertaking reaching further still. Both passages show us Sohrawardî the wanderer, searching for his spiritual family, conscious of the lineage to which he belongs and whose sublime wisdom, he repeatedly declares, he has undertaken to revive.
Yet he is just as conscious that, in pursuing this particular undertaking, he has had no predecessor.
